Apple (DOJ antitrust, filed March 2024): current status, alleged theories, possible remedies and dated next steps; (2) EU Digital Markets Act: App Store and interoperability obligations, any Commission fines, the revised fee structure and its revenue effect; (3) the Google default-search payments (reported at roughly $20bn a year) and how the remedies in the US Google case could remove or shrink them — label the figure's status; (4) US tariffs and Section 232 actions affecting hardware and China-assembled goods, with rates and dates; (5) China market access and India production incentives; (6) ESG: supply-chain labour, carbon-neutrality claims, privacy, board diversity and any controversy record.

> Research questions: (1) iPhone roadmap and the FY2025-26 cycles (iPhone 17 and 18 timing, foldable timing, ASP and mix); (2) Apple Intelligence: what shipped versus slipped, the Siri overhaul status, third-party model partnerships and their economics; (3) the Apple silicon roadmap versus Qualcomm, Intel and AMD, and what it does to gross margin and product differentiation; (4) wearables, Vision and health products as growth vectors; (5) patent filings and R&D spend as evidence of the moat. Use dated sources.

> S9 Strategy — decision question: does Apple's strategy convert AI and services into growth without ceding platform control?
> Research questions: (1) capital allocation priorities (buybacks versus R&D versus M&A); (2) India and Vietnam manufacturing shift progress and cost; (3) services strategy and the response to EU DMA obligations; (4) AI infrastructure approach — partner versus build — and its capex implication; (5) the partnerships that matter for the next cycle.
>
> Counter-evidence to seek: AI talent departures, Siri delays, absence of cloud-scale AI capex, dependency on Google or OpenAI, and any evidence the AI story is marketing rather than product. Peers: Samsung, Google, Microsoft, Huawei.

> Registries: USPTO Patent Center and PatentsView, Apple Newsroom and developer documentation, European Commission DMA filings. Policy lens is material; coordinate factual regulatory points with the Regulatory Analyst rather than duplicating them.

> Counter-evidence to seek: services deceleration, a regulatory hit to App Store margins, hardware price elasticity, debt-funded buybacks and buyback-led EPS, FX and China mix. Peers: Microsoft, Alphabet, Samsung Electronics.

> Research questions: (1) liquidity: average daily volume, index weight and free float; (2) total-return decomposition: dividend plus buyback yield plus growth; (3) catalysts and timing that would re-rate the stock; (4) sell discipline and the price at which the risk/reward turns negative; (5) what the bear case implies for peak-to-trough drawdown.
>
> Counter-evidence to seek: multiple compression in a higher-rate regime, growth deceleration toward GDP, a regulatory hit to the services multiple, and valuation support that depends on buybacks rather than organic growth. Peers: Microsoft, Alphabet, Samsung Electronics, Xiaomi.
>
> Use timestamped market data plus SEC filings for the fundamentals; state explicitly where a metric is an estimate. Save your evidence block before drafting.

> **Apple bear-case scoping — four findings that should shape the thesis table**
>
> **1. Component cost, not China or AI, is the live risk.** Q3 FY26 gross margin of 50.1% included ~2pp from tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS [S17]; Q4 guidance points to a step-down (47–48% reported), and the 10-Q says memory, NAND and DRAM cost pressure "may materially negatively impact" margin [S6]. TrendForce puts the 256GB iPhone 18 Pro BOM +38% year on year, with memory 34% of BOM versus ~10% a year earlier [S99]. Each 100bp of gross margin is roughly $0.27 of EPS.
>
> **2. The China bear case is stale.** Greater China was $18.8bn, +22% year on year, in Q3 FY26 [S17]. Apple's Q3 2026 China share rose to 19.5% from 14.7%, second behind Huawei's 21.3%, in a market down 10% [S96]. > Financials is re-saved at revision 8 (8,991 characters; section check passes, no findings); `business_model` is unchanged at revision 4 and carries no FCF or yield figure.
>
> **1. Itemisation.** TTM free cash flow $136,683M [S5, S6] − [$14,101M TTM "other current and non-current liabilities" line (FY2025 −$11,076M + 9M FY2026 $10,016M − 9M FY2025 −$15,161M) − $2,502M clean three-year average (FY2023 $3,031M, FY2024 −$248M after the $15.8B State Aid accrual, FY2025 $4,724M after its settlement)] = **$125,084M**. Zeroing the line gives $122,582M; its best clean year ($4,724M) gives $127,306M. The "$2.2-4.7B gap" is therefore the normal run-rate assumption, not un-itemised items, and $127.3B is the band's top rather than a correction to its middle.
>
> **2. Deferred-consideration test.** The $10.0B cap does not hold: the cash-flow line nets current and non-current other liabilities, and other current liabilities fell $4,128M ($66,387M to $62,259M), so the $13,531M non-current build (to $55,080M) fits inside the $10,016M line; the combined $9,403M build reconciles within $613M. If the whole build is deferred consideration, the figure is $123,152M. **$117.3B would need a $19,383M strip — more than the $14,101M line or the $13,531M build contains — so it is not the floor.**
>
> **3. What the section now states.** Central **$125.1B**, the midpoint of a $122.6-127.3B band named once: **0.97x** conversion, **2.5%** yield, **40.5x** P/FCF; **72.4%** capital-return cover on normalised nine-month FCF, not 67.0%. The deferred-consideration case is $123.2B, 41.2x.
>
> Told the Valuation Analyst (N33); answered the Red Team (N34). The FY2026 10-K must settle the $13.5B intangibles question.

> ## The call
>
> **Watchlist, zero position today.** At **$344.63** on 30 October 2026 — a **$5,029.6bn** market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares — Apple trades at **39.5x trailing** and **35.2x forward** earnings. Staged entry: first tranche of **0.75–1.0% of the fund at $270**, a second tranche to 2.5–3.0% at **$245**, position cap **5% below $225**, sell review above **$380** (38.8x), sale on valuation alone above **$440.6** (45x forward).
>
> **The thesis in two sentences.** Apple is a genuine cash compounder — $466.8bn of trailing revenue, $128.9bn of net income, 0.97x cash conversion on capex of 2.2% of revenue, $62,173m of net cash, and services earning 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue — but at $344.63 the price capitalises the June quarter's **50.1% gross margin**, two points of which were tariff refunds, and no point of the valuation grid reaches the spot price. It belongs on the watchlist as a quality franchise whose entry is a price, not a narrative: the probability-weighted value is **$292**, 15.3% below the price, and the base case of **$284** (29x FY2027 EPS of $9.79) is a multiple call rather than an operating forecast.
>

## Final report

# Apple Inc.: Investment research report
Rating: Watchlist
Composite score: 6.0
Data as of: 2026-10-30

## Executive Briefing

Apple closed at $344.63 on 30 October 2026, a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation on 14,594m basic shares and a 27.5% total return over twelve months; the last reported period is the June quarter, with Q4 FY2026 results due on 2 November 2026, so the price contains no post-results adjustment. The market it trades in is near its high: the S&P 500 at 7,580.07 is up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its record, the Nasdaq is 8.2% below its high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, and the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93%. Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.97 times net income, 0.95 times at the low end of the normalised band, on capex of 2.2% of revenue; it holds $62,173M of net cash and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48%. Three things make it a compounder rather than a cyclical: 65% of premium phone units, a 2nm A20 Pro with an in-house C2 modem in the silicon stack, and a services line earning a 76.3% gross margin that covers all research and development 2.1 times over — the positives the price has already noticed [S6, S17, S113].

The price is the problem. At 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings — the latter on this report's own FY2027 build of $9.79 — against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares sit above every rate point in the report's valuation grid. The discounted cash flow gives $277 at an 8.5% cost of equity on a 35% operating margin and 14% initial growth, $212 at 9.0% on 33% and 9%, and $133 at 9.5% on 30% and 4%; on the base operating case the rate grid gives $229 at 8.5% and $193 at 9.5%, so 50 basis points is worth 8-12% of value, not a third of it. The sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year forward mean of 31.0 times gives $303. The base case is $284, which is 29 times $9.79, and the 18% gap to the price is a multiple call rather than an operating forecast: at 31 times fair value is $303 (-12%), at 33 times $323 (-6%), and at 35 times $343, the price. Two facts would change the call: a gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche at $270, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it, and an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear case toward the cash-flow floor of $133 [S7, S17, S76, S97, S146].

The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise — but the claim rests on our own forecast, not on a consensus estimate. Two aggregators put the median sell-side target near the spot price, evidence this report rates low confidence, and no dated consensus gross-margin or EPS figure is in the register; the difference we claim lies in the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not in the quality of the installed base.

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The probability-weighted value sits below the price, and the full Kelly on the scenario inputs runs to several times any single-name limit, which is why the cap is a risk-budget decision rather than a sizing output. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version. The follow-up diligence is threefold: the working-capital and intangibles note in that filing, a primary consensus feed against which to test the FY2027 build, and the D.C. Circuit briefing and decision.

Will the Google default-search payment survive the D.C. Circuit appeal, and at what annual rate?

The payment is the largest single item in services and runs at near-pure margin. A ban or a materially lower rate resets the services multiple that carries most of the valuation and moves fair value from the base case toward the bear case, regardless of how well the hardware cycle trades.

1. Watchlist, not ownership: at $344.63 the shares trade at 35.2 times forward earnings against 18.09 for the index, and the 18% discount in the base case depends on a 29 times exit, itself 18% below today's multiple [S7, S97, S146].
2. The franchise is not the problem: services earn 40.3% of gross profit, cash conversion is 0.97x, 0.95x at the band floor, and net cash is $62,173M, so a 30% revenue fall leaves the company solvent [S6].
3. The entry is a price, not a narrative: 0.75-1.0% at $270, a second tranche at $245 and the 5% cap below $225, with $270 above the $241 bear case and a 1.5% maximum loss at the cap [S6, S7].

## Company Overview

Apple is legally and structurally clean enough to hold for years — one share class, one registrant, no VIE and a genuinely unblocked exit — but its governance has barely refreshed in a decade and two of seven independents sit at Apple's own age-75 ceiling, so the holding should be underwritten on cash generation and clean title rather than on board quality. Apple Inc. is a California corporation incorporated on 1977-01-03, listed on Nasdaq under AAPL in US dollars. At 2026-01-02 it had 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding against 50,400,000,000 authorised, all of a single class of $0.00001 par common stock with one vote per share. There is no dual-class structure, no VIE, no nominee shareholder and no contractual control chain — verified in the balance sheet and the 2026 proxy, not assumed. Float is effectively the whole company: directors and officers hold 9,079,765 shares, or 0.06%, leaving 99.94%. Vanguard (9.63%) and BlackRock (7.10%) are the only disclosed 5% holders — and BlackRock's figure rests on a Schedule 13G/A reflecting holdings at 2023-12-31, so the 2026 register is partly unknown. ### The entity map is simple; the profit map was not

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Controller | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple Inc. | California, US | Corporation (registrant) | Group parent; designs, sells, holds IP | 100% of group | No controlling holder | S5, S11 |

| Apple Operations Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Irish operations | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Distribution International Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Non-US distribution | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |

Every listed subsidiary is wholly owned; Exhibit 21 omits entities that are not significant in aggregate, so no complete group list is public, and the 10-K does not say which two Irish subsidiaries held the branches at issue. The structure that mattered economically was profit allocation, not ownership: Irish branches operated under tax opinions issued in 1991 and 2007, which the Commission treated as state aid on 2016-08-30. The General Court annulled that decision on 2020-07-15, the Court of Justice set the annulment aside on 2024-09-10, and Apple booked a one-time $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024 — $15.8bn payable to Ireland from escrow, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit. Irish law had already closed the opinions from January 2015. Two consequences follow: the tax rate is now policy-driven rather than engineered, at 24.1% in FY2024 and 15.6% in FY2025 with no filing supporting a return to the pre-2015 structure; and the entity map carries no enforceability premium, because the legal risk attached to it is regulatory rather than structural — a materially better position than a contractually controlled China VIE. [S5]

### Business model: one platform, one rent, one budget owner

Apple sells integrated hardware to consumers, small businesses, education, enterprise and government, then monetises the installed base through Services. FY2025 net sales were $416,161m, split $307,003m products and $109,158m services, with 40% direct and 60% indirect distribution. The end user is usually the buyer, but the budget owner for the highest-margin line is the developer and the subscriber: Services earned a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products. Growth comes from installed-base expansion and price/mix, not unit share — Apple states it holds a minority share of global smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 iPhone was 53.9% of revenue against 51.2% a year earlier and Services 25.2%, so concentration is rising again rather than falling. [S5, S17]

### Governance: senior, stable, slow to refresh

Eight directors stood in 2026: seven independent plus the CEO. Independent tenure averages 12.0 years — Levinson 26 years and chair since 2000, Jung 18, Sugar 16, Wagner 12, Lozano and Gorsky 5, Austin 2 — and two of the seven (Levinson, 75; Sugar, 77) are at or past the company's own guideline that directors generally may not stand for re-election after 75. Committees are conventional and fully independent: Audit under Sugar (nine meetings in 2025), People and Compensation under Jung, Nominating under Wagner; 92% of votes cast supported say-on-pay in 2025. From 2026-09-01 the structure shifts in a way that matters: Ternus joins as CEO and Cook becomes Executive Chair, taking non-independent directors to two of nine (77.8%) and replacing an independent chair with a lead independent director. [S11, S56]

### A clean structure is not a clean earnings record

The forensic problem is optical, not legal. FY2025 returned $106.1bn — $90.7bn of buybacks and $15.4bn of dividends — against free cash flow of $98.8bn, or 107% of it, while diluted EPS rose 22.7% against an 8.0% rise in operating income and the effective tax rate fell to 15.6% from 24.1%. Diluted shares fell 6.9%, from 15,812,547,000 in FY2023 to 14,714,676,000 in Q3 FY2026, and $263.2bn of buybacks over three years bought the arithmetic. That is how a mature hardware company reports high-teens EPS growth; it is also what stops working the year the buyback slows. Counter-evidence is genuine: Q3 FY2026 revenue grew 16% and gross margin reached 50.1%, so FY2026 is not an optical year; no audited FY2026 accounts had been filed on 2026-10-31. [S5, S17]

### Where the judgement breaks, and what to settle

Three events would change the call: a structural remedy in the DOJ monopolisation suit or the DMA Article 6(4) file that reaches commission economics would compress the 75.4% services margin; a board that keeps the executive-chair arrangement past 2027 would entrench a post-CEO chair; and a buyback slowdown would expose the underlying operating growth rate. Confidence is high on identity, ownership and capital-return facts and medium on the board's appetite for refresh, because its own age guideline is already being waived for two members. Diligence should settle whether that waiver was formal and who chairs the board after 2027; whether BlackRock's stake has moved since 2023; what share of Services revenue depends on US third-party payment rules; and the FY2026 buyback pace under the $100bn authorisation of 2025-05-01. [S11, S5]

## Founding Team & Key Personnel

The team is deep in the functions that built the iPhone era — hardware, operations, finance — and thin where the next era is being decided: AI accountability was reorganised in December 2025 into Craig Federighi's software organisation, the chip chief was promoted in April 2026 into a single hardware remit carrying both silicon and hardware engineering, and the new CEO is a hardware engineer who has never run a services or regulatory fight, so the platform is being defended by continuity rather than by a bench built for the transition. Apple is run by career insiders — Cook has been at the company since March 1998 (28 years), Ternus since 2001 (25 years), and the 2025 CFO and COO appointments were internal promotions. Srouji's hardware and silicon organisations invent; Cook built worldwide sales before 2005 and O'Brien runs retail; Cue's organisation holds the App Store rent; Parekh allocates the capital, $106.1bn returned in FY2025; Federighi's software organisation took over AI on 2025-12-01. Pay is where the team is most unusual. Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m — a $3m salary unchanged since 2016, a $6m target cash award and a $50m equity award, 75% performance-based — against Satya Nadella's $96.5m reported for Microsoft's fiscal 2025 and Sundar Pichai's $10.9m reported for 2025, though Pichai's 2026 target equity award is $210m and a 1,348,607-share 2022 award vested to him in February 2026. Apple's other named executives each target about $23m: $1m salary, a 200% cash target and $20m of equity. There are no employment contracts, no change-of-control payments and time-based RSUs vest over roughly four and a half years, so retention runs through unvested stock rather than contractual protection — cheap for shareholders and defensible at 92% say-on-pay, but exposed where pay is undisclosed. [S11, S129, S125]

**The AI organisation has been rebuilt around software, but no filing names an owner of the AI P&L.**
On 2025-12-01 Apple announced that John Giannandrea, SVP Machine Learning and AI Strategy, was stepping down to advise before retiring in spring 2026; Amar Subramanya joined as VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi, taking Apple Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety, while the rest of the organisation moved to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. Siri AI reached users only as a beta in English with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14, running on a Gemini model licensed from Google — delivery, but through a structure in which model, product and commercial accountability sit with three different executives. Hardware, by contrast, has one owner: Srouji's April 2026 appointment put silicon and hardware engineering together. [S127, S113, S111, S133]

Silicon is where the continuity case is strongest and the key-person risk now concentrates. In December 2025 Johny Srouji, then SVP Hardware Technologies and architect of Apple silicon, was reported to have told Cook he was considering leaving. On 2026-04-20 Apple named him Chief Hardware Officer, effective immediately, a newly created role folding the Hardware Engineering organisation Ternus had run into his Hardware Technologies remit, reporting to CEO Ternus; it supersedes the departure report and reads as the retention move that keeps the silicon bench. It also puts product design engineering, silicon, batteries, cameras, displays and modems under one executive with no disclosed succession and, as a non-Section 16 officer, no pay, equity or retention award in the proxy. Custom silicon is the mechanism behind product differentiation and the 36.8% products gross margin, so the concentration is the price of keeping it. [S131, S133, S141, S5, S11]

The 2024-26 turnover cluster is the part a reference check should attack. Within about eighteen months Apple changed CFO (2025-01-01), COO (2025), general counsel (2026-03-01, with Adams retained for government affairs until late 2026), AI leadership (2025-12-01), environment leadership (announced 2025-12-04) and CEO (2026-09-01). Apple calls each a planned transition and two successors were internal, which is real bench evidence; but keeping the outgoing general counsel on government affairs signals how heavy the regulatory load has become, and the general counsel who oversaw those defences is leaving while the DOJ and DMA cases are live. [S11, S128, S132]

What public records confirm is narrow and clean: titles, dates, pay, the $59m target, the 2,162% cumulative TSR under Cook and the 92% say-on-pay. What they contradict or cannot settle is larger — no degrees for six of seven executives, no pay or ownership for Federighi, Cue, Srouji or Joswiak because they are not Section 16 filers, no disclosed succession or retention terms for Srouji's consolidated hardware role, and no named AI owner. For a people-dependent thesis that is a real information discount. Diligence should verify Ternus's non-hardware operating scope and any retention award, Srouji's succession plan and retention, the 2026 awards to non-NEO SVPs, and who signs off the AI roadmap and budget. Apple's leadership biographies would settle degrees and prior employers but were not accessible, so those cells are recorded as not disclosed rather than inferred. [S41, S11]

## Technology & Product

Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a 2.5-billion-device installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer this cycle sells on is rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capex fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026; the standard iPhone 18, 18e and Air 2 are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was cut to $899. Selling the 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March turns one spike into two, and the A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm plus the in-house C2 modem are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. At a fixed price a node advantage becomes margin or performance, and insourcing the modem removes a royalty and gives control of cellular power and cost. The offset is memory: the June 2026 filing expects semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints to intensify, and products gross margin already leans on tariff refunds that will not recur. Prices rose into that memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test. [S112, S6]

| Dimension | Apple | Google | Samsung | Huawei | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Silicon | In-house A-series, 2nm | In-house Tensor | External suppliers | In-house Kirin | S113, S112 |
| Frontier model | Licensed Gemini | Owns Gemini | Licenses Google | In-house stack | S111 |
| AI compute | Rented Google TPUs | Own TPUs and datacentres | Rents cloud | Domestic cloud | S118 |
| AI organisation | Under Software Engineering since 2025-12-01 | DeepMind | Own research | Own research | S127 |

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as an English beta, five more languages promised for October — 23 months after Apple Intelligence shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year; neither confirmed the price. Apple contributes the interface, personal context, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Ownership moved first: on 2025-12-01 Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety passed to software chief Craig Federighi, with Amar Subramanya as VP of AI, as John Giannandrea stepped down ahead of retirement. Apple bought what it could not ship. [S111, S122, S127]

**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed on 2026-01-12 a multi-year deal to supply Gemini for the rebuilt Siri, reported at $1bn a year, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface; not the model or the compute. [S111, S118]

### The licence is small per device and dangerous per query

At the reported $1bn a year the Gemini licence is 0.65% of the $154,859M trailing operating income and $0.06 of EPS, below the $0.52 that 200 basis points of gross margin are worth. Across the 2.5 billion active devices Apple disclosed on 2026-01-29, $0.50, $1 and $2 per device a year cost $1.25bn, $2.5bn and $5.0bn, taking EPS to $0.07, $0.14 and $0.28; booked as a service they would cut services gross margin from 76.3% to 75.3%, 74.2% and 72.2%. The $1bn implies $0.40 a device. Apple does not disclose the classification; R&D up 33% on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence" while capex fell points to R&D, and the choice changes the margin narrative, not EPS. The tail is per-query pricing: at an assumed 1 billion queries a day each cent is $3.65bn a year; Apple discloses neither volume nor rate. [S6, S111, S152]

The replication test favours hardware: a funded team of fifty with every published patent could match a Duo-class hinge in a few years and an A-series-class chip only after a full node cycle, and would still lack the installed base; the assistant can be licensed, as Apple did.

### Wearables, health and Vision are optionality, not a second engine

Health is the most credible adjacency: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny in *Hypertension*, which questions their accuracy; a monthly alert is not a measurement, so the claim is narrow. Vision Pro sits inside Wearables with no disclosed revenue and no confirmed successor. Both add upgrade reasons and are sold as features, not platforms with their own economics. [S124, S5]

If Siri AI leaves beta with usage data showing its integration beats standalone assistants, the layer is worth more than a licensed feature; silence after 2026-11-02 confirms this reading. If the Gemini term is a bridge to its own model, the dependency is temporary. Until then the technology case rests on silicon, yield and switching costs, and the AI case rests on distribution. Confidence is high on machine facts, medium on model economics, low on patents.

## Market & Industry Analysis

Apple's markets are large but no longer volume-growth markets: the smartphone unit pool is contracting at the fastest rate on record in 2026 while its dollar value rises, so revenue growth to 2030 must come from holding more than 40% of smartphone value, monetising a record installed base through services, and a foldable and AI-driven upgrade cycle, not from market growth. Apple's revenue compounded at 3.3% from FY2021 to FY2025 ($365.8B to $416.2B) and then accelerated to 16% in the first nine months of FY2026, with iPhone revenue up 22% [S5, S6].

| Measure | Figure | Period | Method and note | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Global smartphone units | 1.26B | 2025 | Counterpoint full year; Omdia 1.25B | S92 |
| Global smartphone units | just over 1.0B | 2026E | IDC, -16.7%, steepest fall on record | S84 |
| Global smartphone market value (device TAM) | $613B | 2026E | IDC, +6.3% YoY | S84 |
| Global smartphone ASP | $581 | 2026E | IDC, +27.6%; Omdia independently $565 (+21%) | S84, S88 |
| Premium segment (wholesale ASP $600+) | 29% of global units | H1 2026 | Counterpoint; 25% in H1 2025, 20% in H1 2022 | S94 |
| Apple iPhone revenue | $209.6B FY2025; $196.5B 9M FY2026 | FY2025 / 9M FY2026 | Apple filings; +22% in 9M FY2026 | S5, S6 |
| Apple share of smartphone value | 36% FY2025; 42.7% annualised 2026 | FY2025 / 2026 | Calculated: iPhone revenue / (units x ASP) | S5, S6, S92, S88 |
| Wearables units | 625M | 2026E | IDC; 2.4% CAGR to 687M by 2030 | S85 |

Two independent methods agree the market grows in dollars while shrinking in units, and sizing stacks into three layers. TAM: top-down, IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0B units, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613B because average selling prices jump 27.6% to $581; Omdia independently forecasts ASP rising from $467 in 2025 to $565 in 2026, a 21% increase it calls the largest on record [S84, S88]. SAM: the premium segment (29% of units at $600 or more) plus the iOS installed base for services, where Apple's 65% premium share sets the addressable pool. SOM: Apple's current capture, $466.8B of trailing-twelve-month revenue to June 2026, of which $245.5B is iPhone and $120.5B services. Bottom-up, 1.0B units at $581 imply $581B, within 5% of IDC's value line. The mechanism is a memory cost shock: IDC puts NAND and DRAM costs more than 300% above a year earlier, and the increase is passed through to shelf prices; the market is not expanding, it is being repriced.

Apple's revenue sits where the market is concentrating. Premium handsets reached 29% of global unit sales in H1 2026, up from 25% a year earlier and 20% in H1 2022, and Apple took 65% of those premium units with 9% growth [S94, S92, S84, S5, S6, S88]. Its all-vendor unit share was 20% in 2025, and IDC expects iOS share to reach a record 23.6% in 2026 as Android shipments fall 24.3%. On my calculation Apple captured 36% of global smartphone value in FY2025, $209.6B of iPhone revenue against a $588B market at a $467 ASP, and annualising nine-month FY2026 iPhone revenue gives $262B, or 42.7% of IDC's $613B 2026 value. Value capture, not unit share, is the franchise an investor is buying.

The durability test is whether that value capture survives a 20-30% price increase, and full-cycle elasticity is not established. Apple's product gross margin rose to 40.1% in Q3 FY2026 from 34.5% on richer mix and tariff refunds, and revenue grew in every segment in double digits, but that is margin evidence, not elasticity evidence. Two launch windows point to low elasticity: CIRP's US weighted average retail price reached a record December-quarter $1,077 after the $100 iPhone 17 Pro increase, and iPhone 18 Pro sales rose 23.5% in three weeks after a further $100 rise; both are mix-led and launch-bound, so they are anecdotes, not proof. IDC attributes part of the China strength to buyers pulling purchases forward ahead of Apple's own second-half price increases and warns China's decline could widen to 20% in H2 2026. The sub-$100 segment, 173M units in 2025, fell nearly 60% in Q2 2026. A market that grows in dollars while shrinking in units can flatter Apple for four to six quarters and then mean-revert; the base rate is the 3.3% revenue CAGR of FY2021-FY2025, not the 16% of the last nine months [S17, S87, S84, S150, S96].

Three pools can add revenue to 2030, and only one can change the trajectory [S84, S6, S83, S89, S85, S95]. Foldables: Apple enters in H2 2026, and IDC expects more than 17M foldable iPhones by 2027 at an ASP above $2,550, 40% of a category worth $45.7B. Services: $120.5B trailing twelve months to June 2026, growing 14.1% in nine months at a 76.3% gross margin, against a $1.34T advertising pool in 2026 and $149B of App Store digital goods in 2025. Wearables and PC: wearables grow 2.4% a year to 2030, with smartwatches down 3.7% in 2026 and glasses up 18.1% a year, and the Mac gained share to 9.9% in a PC market down 4.9%. The non-phone pools, $33.7B of Mac and $35.7B of wearables in FY2025, are too small to carry group growth alone.

Geography splits the durability question, and policy is a live variable in every region [S6, S87, S77]. Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue but produced 30% growth in the first nine months of FY2026; Europe is 26.7% and grew 16%, the Americas 42.9% and 11%, Japan 6.9% and 10%, and Rest of Asia-Pacific 8.1% and 19%. The China number is the most fragile in size, not share: the market fell 10% in Q3 2026 to the lowest third-quarter level since 2012, yet Apple's share rose 4.8 points to 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, and the top six vendors hold 96%. The EU's DMA terms cut the commission on externally distributed digital transactions to 5% from 1 October 2026. US tariffs moved twice in 2026: the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 20 February 2026 and Section 301 duties were imposed since, while the Section 232 semiconductor review produced no additional tariffs on Apple products on 14 January 2026. Demand is organic consumer replacement, not policy-created: China's subsidies faded in 2026 and India's incentives are supply-side manufacturing support. The budget owner is the consumer or carrier financing plan; the procurement cycle follows the annual September launch; willingness to pay is being tested by the 27.6% ASP increase. What would change the conclusion: services growth above 15% with user growth, a foldable cycle adding IDC's $45.7B category value, or China stabilising after H2 2026. Confidence is high on 2026 data and low on 2027-2030 regional sizing, because regional market values are paywalled and Apple does not disclose units; the open questions are what share of iPhone growth is units versus price, whether services growth is users or price, how much China demand was pulled forward, and how much memory cost Apple can pass through in FY2027.

**Apple's markets are growing in dollars while shrinking in units, so its growth is price- and share-led, not market-led.**

The global pool is $613B of smartphone value in 2026 against just over 1.0B units, with a 27.6% ASP increase doing the work volume used to do (IDC, S84). Premium concentration (29% of units) and Apple's 65% share of it explain why Apple captures 36-43% of value on 20-24% of units (Counterpoint, S94; Apple filings, S5, S6). Foldables ($45.7B of category value by 2027) and services ($120.5B TTM at 76.0% gross margin) are the only pools large enough to move group growth; wearables grow 2.4% a year to 2030 (IDC, S85).

## Competitive Landscape

Apple is winning on profit and price and, since the September 2026 quarter, on share in a shrinking China market: a 65% share of premium phone units at a 40.1% product gross margin, Huawei ahead in China 21.3% to 19.5% but Apple up 4.8 points, and regulation capping the services take rate. It is strengthening in hardware, contested in services by OpenAI and Alphabet, and exposed to market size rather than share loss [S5].

Huawei is the most dangerous rival to Apple's profit pool, Samsung to its unit position. Huawei led China 21.3% to 19.5% in Q3 2026, after 22.6% to 18.1% in Q2, and IDC expects HarmonyOS shipments to nearly triple to 51M units in 2026, funded by CNY192.3B of R&D, 21.8% of 2025 revenue [S96, S139, S140, S86]. Samsung is broader, with scale across phones, wearables and PCs, but its MX and Networks division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 despite 10.55% revenue growth. Huawei takes price and Samsung volume, at a loss.

Apple's global smartphone market share was 20% in 2025 to Samsung's 19%, and 22% in Q3 2026 to Samsung's 23%, so its position moves sideways even as value capture rises [S92, S120, S94, S84, S150]. The premium layer is where Apple improves: a 65% share of $600-plus units in H1 2026, and IDC expects iOS to reach a record 23.6% in 2026. Pricing power is partially established, not proven, because part of the price rise is a memory shock, with NAND and DRAM costs more than 300% above a year earlier. The mechanism is mix: a $100 Pro increase lifts revenue per unit even if unit demand is flat. Elasticity evidence is two launch windows: after the $100 iPhone 17 Pro increase in September 2025, CIRP put the US weighted average retail price at a record December-quarter $1,077 against $953, and iPhone 18 Pro sales rose 23.5% in the first three weeks after a further $100 rise. Both are mix-led launch windows, therefore full-cycle elasticity is not established.

China is where risk has flipped from share loss to market contraction [S139, S140, S87, S6]. Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% to the lowest third-quarter level since 2012 (Counterpoint) and 15.4% (IDC); Apple took 19.5%, up 4.8 points, Huawei led at 21.3%, and the two were the only top brands to gain. Apple's Greater China revenue grew 30% in nine months of FY2026. The vulnerability is the pool's size and price level: IDC expects component costs elevated through much of 2027, Apple raised iPhone 18 Pro prices by $100 and holds the standard iPhone 18 to spring 2027, so part of the gain is pull-forward. Apple has steadied China without regaining structural leadership; HarmonyOS still gives Huawei a localisation advantage.

Two competitors sit above the handset fight; neither needs a phone to reach Apple's services wallet [S148, S149, S151, S118]. ChatGPT reached 1.2 billion weekly users by 29 September 2026, and OpenAI told investors it had about $50B of annualised revenue at end-September, 77% run-rate growth in the quarter against Apple's 14.1% services growth in nine months. That is 41% of Apple's $120.5B services revenue. OpenAI is also a future hardware entrant, working with Jony Ive on a device shipping no earlier than February 2027. Microsoft attacks the layer beneath: $331.8B of FY2026 revenue at a 46.8% operating margin and 20% of Q2 2026 cloud spend to AWS's 28% and Google's 15%. Apple buys compute rather than owning it, including Google TPUs, so its AI cost curve depends on rivals.

Regulation transfers rent from Apple to rivals [S77, S102, S93]. From 1 October 2026 the EU applies a 26% commission on App Store in-app purchases and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web, after Apple was fined EUR500M for DMA non-compliance in 2025. That lowers switching costs in a region that is 26.7% of Apple's revenue and gives Spotify and rival storefronts an iOS channel; Spotify has 300M paying subscribers against an estimated 100-108M for Apple Music. Its spread to other jurisdictions is the risk to monitor.

The status quo, doing nothing, is formidable: consumers hold devices longer, the cheapest segment is disappearing, and IDC sees no China recovery before 2028-2029. Pipeline threats: the foldable, HarmonyOS, Gemini-powered Pixel and OpenAI's 2027 device. Apple's wedge is silicon, OS and a record installed base, which means it earns product margins rivals cannot match while they earn single digits or lose money; that supports profit-share gains and 2026 share gains inside a contracting market, but not unit growth. That supports a quality-compounder view with a regulated services ceiling, not a share-gain story. Confidence is medium-high on hardware and China, medium on services. Diligence questions: how much of the premium and China gain is price inflation, how much ChatGPT usage substitutes for Siri, how fast EU developers shift to external distribution, and whether Huawei can export HarmonyOS.

**Apple's competitive advantage is profit capture, and in 2026 also China premium share, not unit leadership.**

Apple holds 20% of units but 65% of premium units and 36-43% of value (Counterpoint, S94; IDC, S84). In China, Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% yet Apple's share rose 4.8 points to 19.5% behind Huawei's 21.3% (Counterpoint, S139, S96); the vulnerability is the shrinking pool and regulation (S140, S77), not lost share. The services layer is contested: ChatGPT reached 1.2 billion weekly users and OpenAI about $50B of annualised revenue (S148, S149).

## Business Model

Apple monetises the same customer twice: once through a hardware sale at a 39.1% trailing gross margin that is paid for before the cost is incurred, and again through a services annuity at a 76.0% trailing gross margin that costs almost nothing incremental to serve. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 the company recorded $466,823M of revenue and $227,123M of gross profit — iPhone $245,540M (52.6% of revenue), Services $120,478M (25.8% of revenue but 40.3% of gross profit), Mac $35,863M, Wearables, Home and Accessories $36,290M and iPad $28,652M. Services gross profit of $91,607M covers total company R&D of $42,901M 2.1 times, so the annuity already pays for the AI build-out. The mix, not the growth rate, is what an investor is underwriting. [S5, S6]

### The 2026 acceleration is hardware, not annuity

In the nine months to 27 June 2026 revenue grew 16.1%, but the engines ran at different speeds: iPhone +22.4%, Mac +8.6%, iPad +3.0%, Wearables +2.3%, Services +14.1%. Services therefore fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% in FY2025 — the first year-over-year decline in the mix since at least FY2023, when services were 22.2% of revenue. Greater China grew 30% after shrinking 4% in FY2025. The standard account of Apple as a services compounder is not what the last three quarters show; they show an iPhone cycle carried by Pro-model mix, with the annuity growing at 14.1% against iPhone's 22.4%. The counterpoint is that 14.1% growth on a $109,158M FY2025 base is $15,391M of incremental annual revenue at a 76.3% margin, more gross profit than most software companies generate in total. [S5, S6]

### What one device earns

Apple stopped disclosing unit shipments, so the most defensible unit is the active device. The table divides trailing-twelve-month flows by Apple's own installed-base statement; because that base is an earnings-call figure rather than a filed one, every line is an estimate.

| of which Services | $48.2 | $120,478M TTM ÷ 2,500M | S6, S73 |
| Gross profit | $90.8 | 48.7% blended gross margin | S6 |
| Selling, general and administrative | ($11.7) | $29,363M TTM | S6 |

The waterfall ends where most hardware businesses begin: there is no customer-acquisition payback period to compute, because Apple is paid by carriers and retailers before it pays its assemblers. Payables of $64,525M against inventory of $11,092M produced a cash conversion cycle of −56.8 days at 27 June 2026, against +39.2 days at Alphabet; each new device is cash-positive on day one. That advantage is not a scale economy a rival can buy with capital — it is the accounting consequence of owning the customer and outsourcing the factory. [S6, S73]

### The annuity rests on two contested tolls

The 10-K describes Services as advertising (including third-party licensing arrangements), AppleCare, cloud, the App Store, subscription content and payment services, but never splits their revenue. Two of those lines are tolls on other people's commerce. The first is the App Store commission: on 11 December 2025 the Ninth Circuit held that Apple's 27% commission on purchases made after a user follows a link out of an app had a prohibitive effect, and remanded for the district court to decide what commission, if any, may be charged. The second is the Google default-search licence, where court records show Apple received 36% of search advertising revenue generated through Safari and a 2022 payment put at $20B — 16.6% of trailing-twelve-month services revenue of $120,478M and 12.9% of trailing-twelve-month operating income of $154,859M; measured on FY2025 the same $20B would be 18.3% of $109,158M services revenue and 15.0% of $133,050M operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy kept the payments but barred exclusivity and capped any default arrangement at twelve months, and Google's D.C. Circuit brief of 22 May 2026 challenges that judgment. [S69, S70]

### The cost side has turned

The 2026 margin record is partly purchased. Nine-month products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% (the June quarter was 40.1%), and the 10-Q attributes the gain to product mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by higher costs including memory; the third-quarter release put the refund benefit at 2 percentage points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Against that, memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 versus the 2025 average, and Samsung's mobile memory costs rose 107%. Apple's filing expects the component trends "to intensify, which may materially negatively impact" revenue, costs and gross margin, and concedes that price increases "may also reduce demand" — the elasticity admission a hardware model has to make. A 47-48% gross margin is the defensible base case, not the 50.1% just printed. [S17, S68]

### What this means for the watchlist

The business is a negative-working-capital hardware engine bolted to a high-margin annuity, and the annuity is the terminal value. That structure justifies a premium to hardware peers but not a software multiple on the whole revenue base, because a quarter of revenue sits in a line where two tolls are being repriced in court, and much of the rest faces a memory cycle that turns faster than Apple can re-price handsets. At $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594.18M shares outstanding at 17 July 2026 — 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, a 2.6% earnings yield. The price already assumes the annuity survives intact and that memory costs are passed through. The open diligence is narrow and decisive: does services growth re-accelerate above 15% without hardware mix; what commission does the district court set on remand; and when does memory pricing peak in supplier guidance? Confidence in the mix arithmetic is high because it comes from filed segment data; confidence in the durability of the tolls is medium, because Apple discloses neither their size nor their terms, and the FY2026 10-K expected alongside the 2 November 2026 results is the document that would close the gap. [S6, S7]

**The services annuity is what the multiple buys, and it is a smaller share of revenue than it was a year ago.**

Services produced $120,478M of trailing-twelve-month revenue — 25.8% of the total but 40.3% of gross profit and 2.1x company R&D — while its revenue share fell to 25.2% in the nine months to 27 June 2026 as iPhone revenue grew 22.4% against services growth of 14.1% (S5, S6, S17). Two tolls inside that line, the App Store commission and the Safari search licence worth 16.6% of services revenue on a 2022 court figure, are both under active legal challenge (S69, S70).

## Financial Analysis

Apple's profit is unusually cash-true. Over the twelve months to 27 June 2026 operating cash flow was $146,724M, capital expenditure $10,041M and free cash flow $136,683M against net income of $128,930M — a headline conversion of 1.06x, or 0.97x on a normalised $125,084M, on capex of 2.2% of revenue, versus peer Microsoft's 0.50x and 34.9% and Alphabet's 0.08x and 33.9%. Revenue grew from $383,285M in FY2023 to $416,161M in FY2025 and $466,823M trailing, with operating margin of 29.8%, 32.0% and 33.2%. Nine months to 27 June 2026 produced a 43.0% incremental operating margin — $21,809M more operating income on $50,662M more revenue. The question is how much of that increment is repeatable. [S5, S6]

### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Nine months reconcile exactly: products gross profit of $108,819M on $272,629M is 39.9%, services $69,963M on $91,728M is 76.3%, summing to the filed $178,782M; the quarter ran at 40.1% and 75.6%. Services earn 40.3% of the trailing $227,123M gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue at 76.0%. The 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of $2.02 EPS to tariff refunds. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S6, S17, S68]

**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS (S17); products gross margin is 39.9% against 36.9%, and memory prices rose 146% (S6, S68).

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M; working capital supplied $16,366M of the gap. The dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities, +$10,016M against −$15,161M a year earlier. Other non-current liabilities rose $13,531M to $55,080M while other current liabilities fell $4,128M to $62,259M, a combined $9,403M build reconciling within $613M; the prior year carries the ~$15.8B Irish State Aid settlement (cash taxes of $37,332M against a $15,381M provision). The line's clean history is $3,031M in FY2023, −$248M in FY2024 and $4,724M in FY2025, a $2,502M average, so the $14,101M it puts into trailing free cash flow is the soft spot. Replacing it with the $2,502M average gives $125,084M, or 0.97x conversion, a 2.5% free-cash-flow yield and 40.2x price to free cash flow on the $5,029.6bn market capitalisation; zeroing the line gives $122,582M and its best clean year $127,306M, so the defensible band is $122.6-127.3B (39.5-41.0x), with $125.1B the midpoint. The $13,270M of gross intangibles added against investing "other" of $1,780M is consistent with the $13,531M build being deferred consideration — an unpaid purchase, making $123,152M the figure, inside the band. Deferred revenue is no cushion at 3.2% of trailing revenue. [S5, S6]

### The balance sheet is not the risk; the asking price is

At 27 June 2026 cash and marketable securities were $146,517M against debt of $84,344M — net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier while $62,094M of stock was retired. FY2025 notes carried $91.3B of principal with $12.4B due within twelve months; leases add $16.8B of fixed obligations and purchase obligations $57.0B of manufacturing plus $29.3B of other commitments. Two items need checking: $2,604M of unrealised securities losses and intangibles of $25,417M net, up from $13,301M, unexplained in the 10-Q. [S5, S6]

### Returns clear the cost of capital several times; the multiple does not clear the risk

ROE of 148.8% and ROA of 36.1% are genuine, and the reported ROIC of 320.6% is an artefact of $146.5B of cash and negative working capital that shrink invested capital to $45,347M. The measure that survives is cash return on book capital: normalised free cash flow of $125.1B over equity plus debt of $191,864M, or 65.2%, compared with 57.3% in FY2025. With the ten-year Treasury at 4.93% and an equity risk premium of 4.5-5.5%, a 9-11% cost of equity is cleared several times; the price is the constraint: $5,029.6bn of market capitalisation on 14,594.18M shares outstanding at 17 July 2026 is 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, a 2.6% earnings yield; the $5,072B figure uses the June quarter's 14,715M diluted weighted-average count, 39.3x. Capital allocation agrees: nine-month buybacks of $62,094M plus dividends of $11,778M equal 67.0% of reported nine-month free cash flow of $110,197M and 72.4% of the normalised $102,057M ($110,197M − $10,016M other-liabilities inflow + $1,876M, nine-twelfths of the $2,502M clean average); net cash rose, and shares fell 1.7% while net income rose 20.0%, so buybacks added 2.4 points of the 22.4% EPS growth. Not a debt-funded buyback story. [S5, S6, S7, S10]

### What the next print has to clear

No audited fiscal 2026 exists: Apple reports the September quarter on 2 November 2026. Guidance is 9-11% revenue growth for the quarter ($111.7-113.7B off $102.5B), iPhone mid-teens; the register's only consensus is iPhone revenue, $252.4B for FY2026 (+20.4% on the $209,586M filed for FY2025) and $277.4B for FY2027 (+9.9%), with no group-revenue consensus held. On trailing figures at a 17.3% tax rate: 200 basis points of gross margin is $0.52 of EPS (6.0%), 500 basis points is $1.31 (15.0%), losing the $20B search payment is $1.12 (12.9%) and a 10% fall in iPhone revenue at 39.9% is $0.55 (6.3%). Gross margin moves the outcome most because it applies to all $466,823M of revenue while a unit miss applies only to hardware. For the investor, earnings quality is not the constraint; the price is. The open diligence: December-quarter gross margin guidance, FY2027 memory contracted at fixed prices, what the $12,116M of net intangibles bought, and what sits in the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities. [S71, S72]

## Funding History & Valuation

Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) its market capitalisation is $5,029.6bn on 14,594m basic shares, 39.0x trailing net income of $128,930M, and its enterprise value is $4,967.4bn, or 39.5x trailing earnings (price over $8.72 diluted EPS) and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn; that price needs either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding: revenue compounded at 3.3% a year over FY2021-FY2025, and the 5.0% five-year figure to June 2026 is flattered by the latest 16.4% quarter. Forward, 35.2x on $9.79 against a twelve-month average of 35.7x, is still a premium: 39.5x trailing against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity — not growth, which is why the discount rate rather than the operating story controls the price [S7, S6, S97, S14].

Samsung and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements; their multiples are not disclosed, so the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, and the September quarter is guided to 9-11% growth. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it against 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price and mix in a shrinking unit market while costs rise; price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle shows [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is what the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure carries an accrual that has to come out. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but it includes $14.1bn from other current and non-current liabilities: +$10.0bn in the nine months to June 2026 and $4.1bn in the September 2025 quarter. The $25.2bn swing overstates it: the prior-year line carried the $15.8bn Irish State Aid settlement. Netting the line to zero, to its $2.5bn three-year average or to its best clean year of $4.7bn gives normalised FCF of $122.6-127.3bn, $125.1bn central — 0.95-0.99x net income, a 2.4-2.5% yield and 40.2x P/FCF on the basic market value (39.5-41.0x band; 40.5x diluted). The $122.6bn floor zeroes the line; reading the $13.5bn non-current build as deferred consideration gives $123.2bn and 40.8x. R&D grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in nine months; capex is 0.77x depreciation. Nine-month buybacks and dividends of $73.9bn cover 72.4% of normalised FCF, against a $100bn authorisation from May 2025. No equity has been raised in the five fiscal years to FY2025: $438.6bn of buybacks and $75.0bn of dividends were funded from cash flow, and debt fell from $124.7bn to $84.3bn [S1, S5, S6].

A discounted cash flow suits a company whose value is almost all terminal, and is the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.1bn (nine months $364.4bn plus $112.7bn at the 10% guidance midpoint), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin and a 17.5% tax rate. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate; on the base operating case, at 4.0% terminal growth, each 50bp on the rate moves value by 8-12%. The question is whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

The weights and the $270 entry price come from this exit-multiple set, not the DCF: the bull row applies 35x to $10.20 on a 34.4% operating margin, and the weights give $291.5, 15% below the price. The 29x and 35x are the report's judgement, not a dated forward series: they bracket the 31.0x four-year mean of Apple's fiscal year-end trailing P/E (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x) and the 35.7x twelve-month forward average. A low-confidence market-data aggregator puts the ten-year trailing P/E range at 9.9x-42.5x and, on the same basis, the 2026-10-22 reading above its 99th percentile. The base case at 29x is 18% below the market only because 29x sits below that mean; at 31.0x the same $9.79 is $303, 12% below, and a three-year hold bought at $344.63 and sold at 31x returns 1.3% a year, as the exit analysis shows. The investor implication is a watchlist place and an entry near $270, not ownership at $344.63; at today's price the shares are a hold only for a holder with a lower basis [S6, S7, S97, S153].

The sum of the parts shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 gives services EBIT of $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The Google default-search payment, put at $20bn a year, is the largest risk inside services; the remedies ruling barred exclusivity without banning it, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

The discount rate is a judgement: a lower cost of equity brings the central case to the market price, and quality franchises have held premium multiples through high-rate periods. What I will not concede is a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, which already sits at the top of its own historical range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. No primary consensus feed for revenue, EPS, free cash flow or a price target is available; the earnings figure is the report's own build and the only street target found is the low-confidence range above.

## Development Strategy

Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle. [S5]

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-06-27, at a gross margin 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 and keeping 27 closures confidential, while challenging the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year, 0.65% of trailing operating income. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb frontier training costs. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android, and Apple's own research, while still credible, sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability. The agreement was confirmed under Tim Cook, who moved to Executive Chairman on 2026-09-01 when John Ternus became chief executive, so execution now sits with Ternus and Federighi's software organisation rather than the negotiators: the contract is continuous, the signatory is not. A supplier that also owns Android has seen Apple slip once, which makes renewal terms the thing to watch — a licence priced per device or per query turns the AI bill into a services-margin item rather than an R&D line. [S111, S98]

| Google Cloud | TPU training capacity for Apple foundation models | 2024, disclosed in Apple's model paper | In use | S118 |

### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta. The leadership answer is now dated: on 2025-12-01 John Giannandrea, senior vice president for Machine Learning and AI Strategy, stepped down ahead of retirement, Amar Subramanya joined as vice president of AI, and Foundation Models, ML research and AI Safety and Evaluation moved into Software Engineering under Craig Federighi, with the rest going to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation folded into a software group while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121, S127]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, giving owners a reason to upgrade and not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside Wearables and has no confirmed successor: a research option, not a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

### What the next twelve months must prove

| FY2026 fourth-quarter results, guided to 9-11% revenue growth | 2026-11-02 | Scheduled | Whether iPhone 18 and Duo demand held through launch | S116 |
| Siri AI out of beta, with five more languages | From 2026-10 | Beta in English since 2026-09-14 | That a licensed model can be made to feel like an Apple product | S113 |

The strategy converts AI into growth through the installed base rather than through the model: a better assistant sells phones and protects high-margin services, and those services pay for the R&D the assistant requires. What must be true within twelve months is narrow and checkable. The December 2026 quarter has to show that higher prices did not break demand; Siri has to leave beta and hold quality in languages beyond English; services growth has to stay in double digits against DMA remedies; and gross margin has to absorb memory inflation without the non-recurring tariff refunds that flattered 2026. If all four hold, the company has bought time and the partnership is a bridge. If two fail, the AI expense is funding a feature that does not defend the price.

The signposts that would show the strategy failing are specific: a discount or a lower-capacity model to hold iPhone volume, a second slip in Siri availability, a fall in services growth below the rate of the installed base, or disclosure of a large multi-year model licence whose cost is not offset by hardware price. None of these is visible in the filings reviewed. The strategic risk is not that Apple loses the AI race on capability — it is that the race turns out not to be the thing that sells phones, in which case Apple wins the hardware cycle and the AI spending was a cost of staying in the conversation.

## Risk Assessment

Apple is a quality compounder priced for a peak margin and a contested services annuity: the risks that matter destroy the multiple, not the balance sheet, and none is priced at $344.63. At that 2026-10-30 price the shares trade at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median; the DCF is $212 at 9.0% cost of equity, $277 at 8.5% and $133 at 9.5%.
